[Messages]
[System]: You are in a written contract discussion between your company and an external vendor regarding a SaaS subscription. The goal is to see if you can reach a mutually acceptable agreement over the next couple of days. You may ask questions, request clarifications, and consult your internal reference materials as needed.

[Counterparty]: Thanks for taking the time to speak with us. We’ve put together an initial proposal for your review.

Here are the key commercial points:
- Service: Enterprise license to our cloud-based data analytics platform for up to 150 named users
- Term: 24-month subscription
- Price: $120,000 per year, billed annually in advance
- Uptime commitment: 99.5% monthly uptime SLA, measured across our production environment
- Support: Standard business-hours email and chat support included; premium 24/7 support available as an add-on
- Implementation: We typically have new customers live within 2 weeks of contract signature; we’re proposing a contractual implementation window of 30 days to account for coordination on your side

Key legal terms:
- Limitation of liability: Capped at 12 months of fees paid under the agreement
- Confidentiality: Mutual NDA provisions embedded in the master services agreement
- Data use: We will have the right to use aggregated and anonymized usage data to improve our services and for internal analytics

We believe this package is very competitive for the functionality and support level we’re offering your team. If you can share a bit about your expected usage patterns and any must-have security or compliance requirements, we can fine-tune the proposal.

Happy to answer any questions you have.

[Advisor]: At a glance, this looks like a fairly standard opening offer for a SaaS deal. From our side, we should pay special attention to:
- How "aggregated and anonymized" data use is defined and whether it could expose patterns about our operations.
- Whether the liability cap and uptime SLA are in line with industry norms for this price point.

You’ll want to get clarity on the data terms and maybe benchmark the liability and SLA against our internal references before we agree to anything.

[System]: Thanks for keeping the discussion moving. There is still ample time within the next couple of days to review clarifications and, if needed, iterate on specific terms before aiming to finalize a draft.

[Counterparty]: Thanks for the thoughtful questions—happy to provide more detail.

On data use: when we say "aggregated and anonymized" usage data, we are referring to metrics such as feature adoption rates, average session duration, and high-level performance statistics across our customer base. Any data we use for internal analytics is either aggregated across multiple customers or stripped of direct identifiers like user names, email addresses, and account IDs. We do retain raw usage logs in a secure environment for up to 90 days for troubleshooting and security monitoring purposes, but those are not shared outside our organization, and we do not sell customer-specific data to third parties. We may share high-level, fully aggregated benchmarks (for example, average query latency by industry) in marketing materials, but nothing that would be traceable to your company.

On uptime: the 99.5% monthly uptime SLA is our standard enterprise commitment today. If we fall below that threshold in a given month, we provide service credits starting at 5% of the monthly equivalent of your annual fee, scaling up to a maximum of 25% depending on the extent of the downtime—those details are laid out in our standard SLA schedule. Uptime is measured across our production environment based on our monitoring tools, excluding scheduled maintenance windows notified in advance.

On liability: capping liability at 12 months of fees, limited to direct damages, is our usual position for customers at this scale, and it aligns with what we see in many peer agreements. That said, for longer-term relationships we have sometimes been able to flex modestly, for example by carving out certain confidentiality or data security breaches from the cap or modestly increasing the cap in exchange for longer commitment.

If you can share which of these areas is most important for you to tighten, we can see what room we have to adjust.

[Advisor]: Their explanations are broadly in line with what we’d expect, but there are a few points I’d keep a close eye on.

The 90-day retention of raw usage logs and the ability to use aggregated benchmarks in marketing could still reveal more about our operational patterns than we’re entirely comfortable with unless the contract language is very tight. The 99.5% uptime and credit structure are not outlandish, but our past deals of similar size have sometimes landed closer to 99.9% or at least stronger credits for significant outages. The 12-month liability cap is common, yet we might reasonably push for targeted carve-outs (e.g., for confidentiality or security incidents) or a somewhat higher cap. I’d suggest you consider asking for more explicit contractual limitations on data use and retention, and think about where we most need additional protection before you signal that we’re broadly comfortable.
